proposed_updates.quote: There was an overall effect of MPH (SMD=0.21, p=.0004)
proposed_updates.robustness: NO confidence interval is reported in the abstract (SMD and p only) and the full text is paywalled on ScienceDirect, so ci_reported=false and no CI was estimated. Signs as reported by the authors (positive = enhancement); no flip applied. Composite of 47 effect sizes from k=24 studies in healthy NON-sleep-deprived adults, driven by recall (SMD=0.43, p=.0002), sustained attention (SMD=0.42, p=.0004) and inhibitory control (SMD=0.27, p=.03); remaining domains (updating, switching, semantic access, spatial working memory, selective attention) were null, so the composite is domain-heterogeneous. Authors' own framing is deflationary: 'effects are small, in experiments that do not accurately reflect their actual use' and 'user perception... is not supported by the evidence so far'. Total participant N is not given in the abstract. DOI 10.1016/j.euroneuro.2020.07.002; Eur Neuropsychopharmacol 2020 Sep;38:40-62. IMPORTANT: the same paper reports 'There were no effects for d-amph' (k=10, 27 effect sizes) but gives NO numeric pooled SMD for d-amphetamine, so no dextroamphetamine row could be extracted - do not infer one. is_update flagged true because searches through 2026 found no newer meta-analysis of MPH in healthy non-ADHD adults; verify against the currently cited source (e.g. Ilieva 2015, PMID:25591060, which does report CIs) before overwriting.
proposed_updates.verifier_note:
ENRICHMENT, NOT A CORRECTION: the claim recorded CI as "not reported," which is true of the ABSTRACT (the abstract gives only SMD and p-values, no intervals). However, the full text DOES report the interval in the results section: 95% CI 0.09 to 0.32. I have supplied those values in corrected_ci_lo/hi so the ledger can carry the real interval instead of a null. This is an omission filled, not a discrepancy found — nothing in the claim was wrong. The verdict remains CONFIRMED.

Additional metadata for the ledger row:
- Full reference: Eur Neuropsychopharmacol. 2020 Sep;38:40-62. DOI 10.1016/j.euroneuro.2020.07.002.
- Effect metric is SMD (Hedges/Cohen-family standardized mean difference), consistent with a g-type ledger field.
- Full test statistics for the pooled MPH effect: Z = 3.54, p = .0004, I2 = 66%.
- k = 24 studies contributing 47 effect sizes. If the ledger's k field means "studies," 24 is right; if it ever means "effect sizes," the correct value would be 47. Flagging because effect-size dependency matters downstream.
- Sample: 501 participants from repeated-measures designs plus 144 from between-groups designs (92 MPH, 92 placebo — note this sub-count is internally inconsistent with 144 in the source text; a minor arithmetic slip by the original authors, immaterial to the pooled estimate).
- Design caveat worth carrying: administration is ACUTE (single-dose), not chronic. Do not generalize this row to sustained-dosing regimens.

CAVEATS FOR ANY DOWNSTREAM INTERPRETATION (methodological, not grounds for rejection):
1. Substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 66%) and a statistically significant test for subgroup differences (chi2 = 18.27, df = 7, p = .01, I2 = 61.7%). The "global composite" of 0.21 therefore averages over genuinely heterogeneous domain effects — it is not a uniform pro-cognitive effect. It is driven by recall (0.43), sustained attention (0.42), and inhibitory control (0.27), while switching (0.02), updating (0.06), spatial WM (-0.14), and selective attention (0.03) were all null.
2. The MPH funnel plot showed visual asymmetry; Egger's test was non-significant at the authors' pre-set liberal threshold (t(46) = 1.62, p = 0.11, criterion p < 0.1) — so "no evidence of publication bias" is a borderline pass, not a clean one.
3. The authors' own conclusion is deflationary: effects are small and "data with these stimulants is far from positive." A ledger row showing +0.21 should not be read as the authors endorsing MPH as an effective enhancer.
4. The overall effect was robust to leave-one-out jackknife removal, but the inhibitory-control subgroup was not (becomes non-significant after removing any of four studies). The pooled 0.21 itself is stable.

_adjudication.reasoning:
ELIGIBLE. (a) Meta-analytic: Roberts 2020 (PMID:32709551) is a series of meta-analyses of acute pharmacological cognitive enhancement; the row carries a pooled SMD=0.21 with CI and k=24, i.e. a pooled estimate, not a single trial. (b) Objective cognitive outcome: the pooled domain is "global" cognitive performance built from objective task-based measures (memory, attention, executive function, processing speed), not mood/fatigue/wellbeing/self-report. (c) Population: healthy adults, explicitly a non-clinical enhancement question. (d) Intervention: methylphenidate is an administered exogenous drug, not a merely-measured endogenous biomarker.

TIER = clean_MA. The recorded "healthy_mixed" label denotes healthy adults pooled across mixed age/sex strata, not a blend of healthy with MCI/dementia/ADHD or other patient samples. Roberts 2020 is scoped to healthy (non-patient) adults, so the estimate is cleanly attributable to healthy adults. I would have downgraded to mixed_pop if any ADHD or cognitively impaired arms were pooled in; there is no indication of that here, so mixed_pop is not warranted.

CANDIDATE_ENHANCER = 1. Methylphenidate is one of the archetypal off-label "smart drugs" — alongside modafinil and d-amphetamine it is the canonical prescription stimulant taken non-medically by healthy students and professionals specifically to raise cognitive performance. It is proposed, used, and studied as an enhancer, not as an impairment/insult state. This is the opposite of the alcohol/dehydration/sleep-deprivation stratum, so it must remain in the primary enhancement analysis rather than being segregated as an impairer.

RED FLAGS. Effect magnitude is small and entirely plausible (SMD 0.21, CI [0.09, 0.32] — significant but modest, exactly what the catecholaminergic enhancement literature converges on), so no implausible_effect_size. CI is reported, so no no_ci_reported. k=24 is a well-powered pool, so no very_few_studies. Population is specified as healthy, so no population_ambiguous. Acute stimulant dosing here is a therapeutic/enhancement dose range, not an intoxication insult, so no acute_intoxication_state. There is no strong conflicting-MA signal — Repantis 2010 and Ilieva 2015 report similarly small positive effects — so "contested" is not justified.

The one flag that does apply is duplicate_of_existing: the curator/verifier note states this is an UPDATE confirming an existing ledger row exactly. The content is eligible and correct, but it should be merged idempotently into the existing methylphenidate/Roberts-2020 row rather than appended as a second row; appending would double-count one meta-analysis and artificially inflate both the row count and the apparent independent evidence base for catecholaminergic enhancement.

proposed_updates.verifier_note:
CI ENRICHMENT (not a mismatch): the ledger records "CI: not reported", which is true of the abstract but not of the paper. The full-text results section reports 95% CI 0.02 to 0.21 (Z = 2.45, p = 0.01). Recommend populating ci_lo=0.02, ci_hi=0.21. This is a fill-in of a blank field, not a correction of a wrong value, so the verdict remains CONFIRMED.

MATERIAL CAVEAT FOR PUBLICATION — the row is numerically accurate but reporting 0.12 as a bare positive pooled effect would misrepresent the source authors' own conclusion:
1. EQUIVALENCE TEST: the authors ran TOST and found the observed effect was significantly WITHIN equivalence bounds of d = -0.2 to +0.2 (Z = -1.65, p = 0.05). They interpret 0.12 as statistically equivalent to zero for practical purposes. Verbatim: "although the TOST procedure indicated that the observed effect size (d = 0.12) was significantly within the equivalent bounds of d = -0.2 and d = 0.2".
2. HETEROGENEITY: I-squared = 72%, high.
3. NO SUBGROUP EFFECT: chi-square = 9.00, df = 7, p = 0.25, I-squared = 22.2% — i.e. no evidence that effects differed by cognitive domain, which weakens the standalone "modafinil improves memory updating (0.28)" subdomain finding.
4. EFFECT-SIZE DEPENDENCY: 64 effect sizes nested within only 14 studies; if the ledger's downstream synthesis treats k as the unit of independent information, 14 is the correct denominator (as claimed), but the original pooling operated at the effect-size level.
5. AUTHORS' OWN FRAMING: "effects are small, in experiments that do not accurately reflect their actual use in the wider population" — they argue the evidence does not support user perceptions of effectiveness.

METRIC NOTE: the reported statistic is SMD (Hedges/Cohen-family standardized mean difference) as labelled by the authors, not explicitly Hedges' g; if the ledger column is strictly typed as g, record the metric as SMD-as-reported rather than silently relabelling.

SIGN CONVENTION: no reaction-time sign flip was needed at the pooled level — the authors already oriented all effect sizes so positive = better cognitive performance.

_adjudication.reasoning:
ELIGIBLE: all three requirements are met. (a) Pooled meta-analytic estimate, not a single trial (SMD=0.12, 95% CI [0.02, 0.21], k=14 studies) from the Roberts 2020 Eur Neuropsychopharmacol series of meta-analyses. (b) Outcome is objective cognitive performance (global/overall composite across memory, attention, executive/updating subdomains from lab tasks), not mood, fatigue, wellbeing, or subjective report. (c) Sample is healthy adult volunteers receiving acute administration — non-clinical. (d) Modafinil is a genuine ingestible pharmacological intervention that a person can take, not an endogenous biomarker merely measured.

TIER = clean_MA: the pooled sample is healthy adults only; there is no admixture of MCI, dementia, ADHD, narcolepsy, or other patient populations. The recorded "healthy_mixed" refers to heterogeneity WITHIN a healthy sample (age/sex/task mix), not to inclusion of impaired participants, so mixed_pop does not apply. I considered "contested" because the modafinil literature has a well-known split (Battleday & Brem 2015 read the evidence as showing enhancement on complex/executive tasks, while Roberts 2020 and Repantis 2010 find trivial-to-null effects) — but that is a magnitude/interpretation disagreement around a small effect rather than a methodological alarm, k=14 is adequate, the effect is small rather than implausibly large, and a CI is reported. clean_MA stands.

CANDIDATE_ENHANCER = 1: modafinil is the archetypal off-label "smart drug" — it is proposed, marketed, and used off-label by healthy people (students, shift workers, military) specifically to improve alertness and cognitive performance. It is an enhancement-intent exposure, not an impairment/insult like alcohol or dehydration, so it belongs in the primary enhancement stratum, not the impairment stratum.

RED FLAGS:
- duplicate_of_existing: this is not a new row. data/raw/healthy_adult_cognition_ledger.csv already contains "modafinil,catecholaminergic,stimulant,overall,0.12,0.02,0.21,14,healthy_nonSD,1,clean_MA,Roberts 2020 Eur Neuropsychopharmacol,PMID:32709551,...,1" — identical effect, CI, k, and PMID. The curator's own note ("UPDATE confirming existing row") agrees. It must be MERGED into the existing row as a re-verification, never appended, or the same Roberts 2020 estimate will be double-counted (note the same paper also supplies the methylphenidate and dextroamphetamine rows, so the three are non-independent and share a common analytic pipeline).
- population_ambiguous: the incoming label "healthy_mixed" is less precise than, and inconsistent with, the ledger's existing "healthy_nonSD". Roberts 2020 analysed healthy, non-sleep-deprived volunteers; the distinction is load-bearing for a wake-promoting agent, since modafinil's largest documented effects occur under sleep deprivation and folding sleep-deprived samples in would change the estimand entirely. Do not let the vaguer incoming label overwrite the existing one — hence suggested_population_label = healthy_nonSD.
- other (two items): (1) TOST caveat — the authors report the pooled effect as statistically EQUIVALENT TO ZERO despite the CI nominally excluding zero (0.12 [0.02, 0.21] is significant but trivially small and inside the equivalence bounds). For predictor scoring this row should be treated as a null/negligible-enhancement anchor, not as a positive enhancement hit; a predictor that confidently calls modafinil a strong enhancer in healthy rested adults should be graded as wrong. The existing ledger's binary enhances_healthy_young=1 arguably overstates this, and the honest reading is "directionally positive, magnitude indistinguishable from zero" — worth carrying as a magnitude qualifier. (2) mechanism_class mismatch — the incoming row says "wake_promoting" while the ledger row says "catecholaminergic / stimulant". Both are defensible for modafinil, but the merge must not silently reclassify the mechanism, since mechanism_class feeds the V7 class-prior machinery (prisma_priors) and the Roberts 2020 g<=0.50 ceiling gate.
No no_ci_reported (CI given), no very_few_studies (k=14), no implausible_effect_size (0.12 is small and consistent with the literature's ceiling), no acute_intoxication_state.

proposed_updates.quote: Significant effects in favor of caffeine were found for both accuracy, g = 0.27, and reaction time, g = 0.28.
proposed_updates.robustness: CIs are NOT reported in the abstract and the article is paywalled (not in PMC/EPMC, isOpenAccess=N), so ci_reported=false and no CI was estimated or reconstructed. Both composite Hedges' g values are reported by the authors as 'in favor of caffeine', i.e. already signed so positive = pro-cognitive; NO sign flip was applied to the reaction-time g. Representative value uses the reaction-time composite (g=0.28); the accuracy composite is g=0.27 - essentially identical, so the choice is not load-bearing. Dose moderation is substantial: >=200 mg outperformed lower doses, with a LINEAR positive dose-response for reaction time but a QUADRATIC one for accuracy (accuracy improves then DECLINES at very high doses) - a genuine sign-flip risk at high dose for accuracy. Effect was NOT moderated by habitual caffeine consumption, task complexity, or which attention network was taxed. Population is rested, healthy adults; pure caffeine only, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled. Scope caveat: attention-only - this meta-analysis does not cover memory or executive function, so it may not fully supersede a broader-domain caffeine row. Psychopharmacology 2025;242(9):1909-1930; DOI 10.1007/s00213-025-06775-1.
proposed_updates.verifier_note:
CI CAVEAT (the one thing I could not fully verify): the claimed CI of "not reported" is accurate at the abstract level — the published abstract genuinely reports bare g values with no interval — but I could NOT confirm whether the full text reports intervals, because the Springer full text sits behind an IDP authorization redirect and the ResearchGate mirror returned HTTP 403. A random-effects meta-analysis of 31 trials will almost certainly report 95% CIs in its Results section and forest plots. So "not reported" should be read as "not reported in the abstract," not as "the paper reports no CI." If the ledger's downstream use requires precision weighting or CI-based heterogeneity handling, this row needs a full-text pull to populate the interval; treat it as a known gap rather than a confirmed absence. This does not affect the CONFIRMED verdict, since a null CI field cannot be a numeric misreport.

SECONDARY FINDINGS from the abstract, available if the ledger wants dose moderators: higher doses (>=200 mg) improved both RT and accuracy more than lower doses; dose-response was positive-linear for RT but quadratic for accuracy (accuracy benefit plateaus/reverses at high dose). Effect was reported as unrelated to habitual caffeine consumption, task complexity, or which attention network was taxed. Total N = 1455 participants across the 31 trials — worth recording alongside k, since 1455/31 implies a mean cell of roughly 47, which is small and relevant to any small-study-effect audit.

ADVERSARIAL NOTE ON WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: the residual 0.05 of uncertainty is not about existence or the numbers — those are pinned by a PMID-keyed API hit plus verbatim quote match. It is that I verified the numbers only from abstract-level text across three renderings of the same underlying abstract, never from the Results section or forest plots themselves. If the full text turned out to report a different primary composite (e.g. a trim-and-fill or outlier-adjusted headline estimate that the abstract does not mention), the row's 0.28 would become the unadjusted figure rather than the paper's preferred one. That is the only realistic failure mode remaining.

_adjudication.reasoning:
ELIGIBLE: ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an ingestible intervention a person can actually take, the row reports a pooled meta-analytic estimate (k=6, g=0.52, CI [0.27,0.78]) rather than a single trial, the outcome is a cognitive performance domain (global cognition, i.e. objective testing rather than mood/fatigue/wellbeing self-report), and the recorded sample is adults who are not a patient population. All three eligibility conditions are met.

CANDIDATE_ENHANCER = 1: ashwagandha is squarely an intentional nootropic/adaptogen — it is commercially marketed (KSM-66, Sensoril) and consumed specifically for stress resilience, memory and focus. It is the opposite of an impairment exposure like alcohol or sleep deprivation, so it belongs in the primary enhancement stratum, not the impairer stratum.

TIER = contested, not clean_MA and not mixed_pop. The population label as recorded ("healthy_mixed") is a healthy-adult label, so mixed_pop is not strictly forced by the recorded sample — but the tier decision is driven by a genuine methodological alarm rather than by population alone: (a) a pooled g=0.52 on GLOBAL cognition from only k=6 studies is a large effect for a botanical supplement and is the classic small-study / publication-bias signature — the ashwagandha trial base is dominated by small, single-site, frequently industry-sponsored studies; (b) the curator/verifier note records that the existing ledger already classifies ashwagandha as contested/mixed_pop on stressed samples, i.e. there are conflicting meta-analytic characterizations of this same compound, which is itself a "strongly conflicting meta-analyses" trigger; (c) the pooled base plausibly blends healthy volunteers with chronically-stressed and sub-clinical-anxiety enrollees, and several ashwagandha syntheses reach into MCI/clinical arms, so clean attribution to healthy adults is not defensible. Contested is the conservative call here because it captures both the population impurity and the effect-magnitude alarm; downgrading only to mixed_pop would understate the small-study risk.

RED FLAGS: implausible_effect_size (0.52 global-cognition effect from 6 small trials); very_few_studies (k=6, below any reasonable bias-detection threshold — Egger/funnel tests are uninformative under k=10); population_ambiguous ("healthy_mixed" plus stressed-sample provenance leaves the healthy-only claim unverified); duplicate_of_existing (the ledger already carries an ashwagandha row per the verifier note — this must be de-duplicated or explicitly superseded before it is scored, otherwise the compound is double-counted in predictor evaluation); other = the supporting quote "improved cognitive outcomes" is non-specific and does not name the instrument or domain, so the objective-performance criterion is satisfied by the recorded domain field rather than by the quote itself — the quote should be strengthened to an instrument-level extract before this row is used as ground truth.

RECOMMENDATION: retain as eligible and as a candidate enhancer, but tier it contested and resolve the duplicate against the existing ashwagandha entry before scoring.

proposed_updates.verifier_note:
Two residual caveats, neither disqualifying, both worth carrying on the ledger row.

CAVEAT 1 - population specificity. The ledger claims population = healthy_young. The abstract supports "healthy adults" for the choice-RT outcome but never says "young." The acute-dose L-theanine cognitive literature is predominantly young-adult samples, but I could not verify an age range from the abstract and the full text is paywalled. Recommend downgrading the row's population label to healthy_adults, or flagging healthy_young as inferred-not-sourced. This does not meet the REJECT_WRONG_POPULATION bar, which targets clinical/patient samples; the parent review does include clinical populations, but the specific pooled estimate being cited is the healthy-adult one.

CAVEAT 2 - k unverified. isOpenAccess = N, inEPMC = N, inPMC = N, hasPDF = N; only fullTextUrl is the paywalled doi.org link, and nature.com 303-redirects to idp.nature.com auth. I therefore could not read the forest plot to extract k or I-squared for the choice-RT analysis specifically. The abstract gives k only for the whole review (31 RCTs, n = 1168), not per outcome. Since the claim lists k = null, there is no asserted value to falsify, and I left corrected_n_studies null rather than guessing. If the ledger later wants k populated for this row, it needs institutional full-text access - do not backfill it from inference.

CONTEXT FOR DOWNSTREAM USE - the effect being cited is the strongest result in the paper, and the paper's other findings are markedly weaker, so the row should not be read as endorsing L-theanine broadly. From the same abstract: acute stress reduction was "modest (SMD = 0.31) and largely influenced by studies with a high risk of bias"; no significant effect on fatigue; anxiety effects "inconsistent and non-significant" apart from a single psychotic-anxiety trial (SMD = 0.54, 400 mg/day x 8 weeks); the depression signal (SMD = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.13-1.25) required excluding one outlier. The choice-RT estimate itself is a single-dose, 200 mg, 30-60 min acute-window effect - it is not evidence for chronic dosing, and the row should record dose/timing conditions if the schema supports it.

VERIFICATION-METHOD FLAG - all evidence here came through WebFetch, which summarizes fetched pages with a small model, so there is nonzero confabulation risk on any single call. I treated that as the main threat and mitigated it by cross-checking four independent endpoints; they agreed on title, all four author surnames, journal, year, and a specific PMID (42410082), and two independently returned the identical abstract wording containing the exact numbers. Independent agreement on a specific PMID is difficult to produce by confabulation. Residual risk is the reason confidence is 0.93 rather than higher; a human spot-check of PMID 42410082 would close it completely.

_adjudication.reasoning:
ELIGIBLE = true. All four eligibility conditions are met: (a) pooled meta-analytic estimate (Gerolymos 2026, Mol Psychiatry, DOI 10.1038/s41380-026-03727-9; parent review 31 RCTs / 1,168 participants), not a single trial; (b) objective cognitive performance outcome — the quoted estimate is choice reaction time (attention/processing-speed domain), a task-based measure, not mood/fatigue/subjective report (notably, the same paper's fatigue, anxiety and stress outcomes ARE subjective and would not have qualified); (c) adults described as healthy for this specific pooled estimate, not a patient sample; (d) l-theanine is an ingestible supplement, a real intervention, not an endogenous biomarker.

TIER = mixed_pop (conservative call, not clean_MA). The parent review explicitly pools healthy AND clinical samples (it reports a psychotic-anxiety trial SMD 0.54 and a depression signal SMD 0.69), and the abstract does not state how many trials or participants contributed to the choice-RT estimate specifically. The verifier could not read the forest plot (isOpenAccess=N, inPMC=N, nature.com auth-redirects), so the composition of THIS pool is asserted by an abstract descriptor rather than demonstrated. Under the ledger's own standard the estimate is therefore "not cleanly attributable to healthy adults" and must not be cited as a healthy-only pooled estimate. This is upgradeable: if a human obtains institutional full text and confirms the choice-RT forest plot contains healthy-adult trials only (with k), the row can be re-tiered to clean_MA. I did NOT use "contested": 0.51 [0.25, 0.77] is a moderate, precise-enough effect (SE ~0.13), not the implausible-magnitude/tiny-k signature, and it does not strongly conflict with the incumbent Payne 2025 estimate for the same outcome (0.35 [0.10, 0.61]) — those CIs overlap heavily, so the two MAs agree rather than conflict.

CANDIDATE_ENHANCER = 1. L-theanine is a textbook marketed nootropic — sold standalone and in caffeine+theanine "focus" stacks explicitly for attention. This is an enhancement-stratum row, not an impairment/insult row, so it belongs in the primary enhancement analysis (subject to its tier).

RED FLAGS:
- population_ambiguous: the row as submitted records "healthy_young", but the source supports only "healthy adults" for this outcome and never says young; age is inferred, not sourced. Separately, the parent corpus contains clinical participants (see tier reasoning). Hence suggested_population_label = healthy_mixed (healthy adults, age composition unverified) rather than healthy_young.
- duplicate_of_existing: this is is_update = true against the curated Payne 2025 row already in data\raw\healthy_adult_cognition_ledger.csv (l_theanine, choice_rt, 0.35 [0.10, 0.61], k=4, clean_MA, PMID:40314930). Same compound, same outcome family, same population claim — it must NOT be appended as a second independent row (that would double-count l-theanine choice-RT in any pooled/scoring analysis) and must NOT silently overwrite the curated row. scripts\122_merge_ledger_expansion.py rule 1 already routes is_update rows to data\raw\provenance\ledger_expansion_2026-07_proposed_updates.json for human decision; that routing is correct and should be respected. Load-bearing consequence a human must weigh: the incumbent l_theanine row IS the project's unique label/rule conflict (CI excludes 0 but labelled null), and tests\test_healthy_adult_robustness.py asserts sens["conflicts"] == ["l_theanine"]. Replacing or relabelling it via this update would move the headline in reports\pipeline\healthy_adult_robustness_v1.md and break that test — an evidence-driven change is legitimate, but it cannot happen as an unreviewed merge.
- other (two items): (1) k is not reported for this specific estimate, so small-study/publication-bias cannot be assessed and the row is not eligible for any k-weighted or power-based analysis; the verifier correctly left it NULL and it must not be backfilled by inference or borrowed from the 31-RCT review total. (2) Outcome-selection/multiplicity exposure — 0.51 is the strongest result in a paper whose other findings are markedly weaker (fatigue null, anxiety inconsistent/non-significant, acute stress 0.31 driven by high-risk-of-bias studies, depression significant only after an outlier exclusion), and the estimate is a narrow acute-window condition (single 200 mg dose, 30-60 min pre-test). It is not evidence for chronic dosing; dose/timing should be recorded on the row if the schema supports it.

I did not flag no_ci_reported (a CI is present) or very_few_studies (k is unknown, and asserting "few" would be a guess — captured under "other" instead). Per instructions I treated the citation as already verified and did not re-verify it.

SOURCE DEFECT FLAG: the published abstract contains an internal inconsistency - attention response time is printed as 'g = 0.86; 95 % CI: 0.53-0.83', a CI that does not bracket its own point estimate (apparent typo in the original); that estimate was therefore NOT used. The accuracy estimate used here (g=0.68, CI 0.48-0.88) is internally consistent. n_studies set to null deliberately: the paper pools EFFECT ESTIMATES, not distinct studies (27 EEs for this outcome), and outcome-level k is not reported; the review as a whole comprised 45 publications and 327 effect estimates. dropped.robustness: IMPAIRMENT: acute cortisol administration worsens working memory; value entered unflipped (negative = anti-cognitive). CI NOT reported in the abstract and full text not accessible — ci_reported=false, nothing estimated. k and N likewise not stated in the abstract, left null. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the abstract does NOT explicitly state that all included samples were healthy adults; acute cortisol-administration studies are conventionally healthy-volunteer designs, but a verifier should confirm the inclusion criteria before this row is treated as healthy-only. The overall (undifferentiated) analyses were nonsignificant; the -0.315 applies only to the rapid/nongenomic window (<~1h post-administration) and the authors state the effects reverse over time (working memory enhanced at longer delay). Same paper: response inhibition ENHANCED g+=0.113, p=.016; set-shifting no effect. DOI 10.1016/j.psyneuen.2015.04.017. Related older meta-analysis (Het 2005, PMID:15919583, Psychoneuroendocrinology, 16 studies / 563 subjects) reports d=-0.49 for cortisol before retrieval (k=4) and d=0.08 before learning (k=12) — converging direction, also without CIs.
dropped.verifier_note:
IMPORTANT INTERPRETIVE CAVEAT (not a rejection, but the row should carry a flag): -0.315 is NOT the overall pooled effect. The abstract explicitly states "the overall analyses were nonsignificant"; -0.315 is the moderated subgroup estimate for the rapid/nongenomic window only (cognitive testing <~1 h post-administration), and the abstract says the effect REVERSED at longer delays (i.e., cortisol enhanced WM >~1 h post-administration). Labeling -0.315 as the "claimed pooled effect" overstates it — it is a delay-moderated subgroup effect selected from a null omnibus analysis. If the ledger's semantics for "pooled effect" mean the headline overall estimate, this row is a selective-reporting hazard and should be relabeled (e.g., effect_scope = "rapid/nongenomic subgroup, <1h post-administration") rather than deleted.

Second caveat: this is EXOGENOUS acute cortisol administration (a stress-hormone challenge), not a cognitive-enhancement intervention. Direction is impairment. For a drug-repurposing ledger this is a negative/anti-nootropic data point and should not be read as evidence that cortisol is a candidate enhancer.

Unresolved: k (number of studies/effect sizes) and CI could not be recovered — full text is paywalled (ScienceDirect returned 403; no open-access PDF located on hmlpubs.faculty.ucdavis.edu or grantsshields.com). Population ("healthy adults") could not be positively confirmed from the methods section; MeSH terms show no clinical population and the design implies healthy volunteers, but this remains inferential. MeSH includes "Animals," which reflects the rodent literature cited to generate hypotheses, not rodent studies pooled in the analysis — do not read this as an animal meta-analysis.

Do not confuse this paper with the adjacent Shields, Sazma & Yonelinas 2016 Neurosci Biobehav Rev meta-analysis ("The effects of acute stress on core executive functions: A meta-analysis and comparison with cortisol"), which is a different paper with different numbers.
